analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a flat 20% tax on wages and business income, exempting investment income entirely.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill never came to a vote: Senator Specter introduced it with zero cosponsors, the Senate Finance Committee held one hearing in May 1995, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the current income tax and replaced it with a single 20% rate. Wages would be taxed after a standard deduction, but interest, dividends, capital gains, and other investment income would be completely untaxed for individuals. Businesses would pay 20% on active business income instead of the up-to-35% corporate rate. It also trimmed deductions people use — capping the charitable deduction at $2,500 and limiting the mortgage interest deduction to $100,000 of home-purchase debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Households living mainly on investment income — interest, dividends, capital gains — would pay no federal income tax on that income at all, since the bill taxed only earned income. Corporations and other businesses would see their top rate drop from 35% to 20%. High earners whose income is mostly from work would still pay 20% on every dollar above the standard deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces graduated income tax rates with a single 20% rate on wages and business income, simplifying the tax code for individuals and businesses. [S2] [S3]
Raises the standard deduction to $16,500 for joint filers with an additional $4,500 per dependent, indexed to inflation, so many lower-wage households would owe little or nothing. [S3]
Cuts the corporate rate from up to 35% to a flat 20% on active business income, with deduction carryovers for loss years. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Salaried and wage workers whose income is entirely earned would pay 20% on all income above the standard deduction, with no lower brackets. The shift of taxation away from investment income and the corporate rate cut would mean large revenue losses, borne by other taxpayers or through cuts to public programs. Homeowners with large mortgages would lose part of their mortgage interest deduction, and donors who give more than $2,500 to charity would lose the deduction on the rest.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill taxes only earned income, a person with millions in dividends, interest, and capital gains would owe no federal income tax, while a worker earning the same amount would pay 20% on every dollar above the standard deduction. [S2] [S3]
The charitable deduction is capped at $2,500 ($1,250 for separate filers), eliminating the tax incentive for larger giving. [S2] [S3]
The mortgage interest deduction is limited to interest on acquisition indebtedness, with the cap cut from $1,000,000 to $100,000, reducing an incentive for home ownership. [S2] [S3]

Supporters' best case was simplicity and an end to the double taxation of saving; the cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge was the shift of the tax burden onto work income and the revenue lost from exempting investment income and cutting the corporate rate. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is real, but the design tilts sharply: all investment income escapes tax while work income is taxed at a flat 20% with no progressive brackets. Combined with the corporate rate cut, the bill would transfer a large share of the tax burden from investors and corporations to salaried workers, or leave a large hole in federal revenue. The modest standard deduction protects only the lowest earners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which held one hearing in May 1995 but never wrote it into legislation or brought it to the floor, and it died when the two-year Congress ended. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter introduced the bill on March 2, 1995, with no cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day. [S1] [S5]
The Finance Committee held hearings on May 18, 1995, its only action on the bill; it was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wage earners came out ahead, since the bill would have shifted taxes onto work income while exempting investment income; homeowners, charities, and federal revenue also avoided the losses the bill would have caused.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill on May 18, 1995, then never marked it up, reported it, or sent it to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Bob Packwood
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held a single hearing on the bill and never advanced it to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan lineup. [S4]

industries.industry: High-income investors and investment income earners
industries.note: The bill taxes only earned income, so interest, dividends, and capital gains would be untaxed, shifting the burden onto wages. Its failure left the current system in place.
The bill would have cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 20% on active business income. Because the bill never advanced, businesses kept paying under the existing corporate tax.
Capping the deduction for charitable gifts at $2,500 would have removed the tax incentive for larger donations, likely reducing giving to nonprofits. The bill's defeat preserved the full deduction.

Limiting the mortgage interest deduction to $100,000 of home-purchase debt would have reduced the subsidy for home ownership and large mortgages. The bill's defeat kept the existing, larger deduction intact.
